newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-GLOBAL SEARCH BEGINS FOR SUCCESSOR TO HAVELANGE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GLOBAL SEARCH BEGINS FOR SUCCESSOR TO HAVELANGE.

text.p: The supremacy of Europe and South America as football's twin power bases may come under attack for the first time in the search for a successor as FIFA president to Joao Havelange following his decision to retire in 1998.

Three potential candidates for the presidency have emerged from Europe -- UEFA president Lennart Johansson, FIFA general-secretary Sepp Blatter and, more intriguingly, Bayern Munich president and former World Cup winner Franz Beckenbauer.

But Africa and Asia have also thrown up potential successors to 80-year-old Brazilian Havelange, who announced on Saturday he would step down after the World Cup finals in France, 24 years after he took the reins of power at soccer's world governing body.
From the Far East comes FIFA vice-president Chung Moon-jung, the man chiefly responsible for bringing half of the 2002 World Cup to South Korea.

Chung, a leading business tycoon and member of the South Korean parliament as well as president of the country's national soccer federation, has been an energetic advocate of his country's bid to co-host the first finals of the 21st century with neighbours Japan.

He has locked horns with Havelange in the past, most notably in November last year when he aimed a stinging rebuke at his boss for visiting Nigeria at a time when the West African country was being condemned across the globe for human rights abuses.
Africa's potential FIFA president is Issa Hayatou, widely-respected head of the African Football Federation -- less vocal than Chung but a natural power-broker and negotiator.

The Cameroonian was instrumental in winning Africa an additional two berths to the 1998 finals in France when the decision was taken after the 1994 U.S. finals to expand the competition from 24 teams to 32.
Five African teams will compete in France as opposed to three in the United States.

The performances of Cameroon and Nigeria in the last two World Cups and at this year's Olympic Games in Atlanta have greatly raised the profile of black African soccer around the world and some will feel the time is right for an African to rule at FIFA headquarters in Zurich. How much support Hayatou has outside Africa remains to be seen.

If either Chung or Hayatou do decide to stand in what will be a straightforward one-country-one-vote ballot, they will undoubtably face opposition from at least one of the big guns of European soccer politics.
Until recently, UEFA chief Johansson, often at odds with the autocratic Havelange, had been considered favourite to take over from the Brazilian.
But the Swede, who said a long time back he would run for the job when Havelange stood down, has done himself no favours recently.

Firstly he chaired a FIFA committee which angered Scotland by unexpectedly ordering them to replay a World Cup tie with Estonia which was cancelled in October after a farcical row over the kick-off time.
Then, far more seriously, he incurred the wrath of soccer's brightest emerging nation by describing Africans as "blackies" in an interview last month with a Swedish newspaper.

Although he subsequently stressed he is not a racist and apologised for his comments, uttered on the eve of the European Community's "European Year against Racism" in 1997, a feeling remains that the Swede is maybe not the man to guide soccer's global family into the 21st century.
By 2006, when Johansson would be eight years into his reign if he succeeded Havelange, an African nation could well be hosting, and maybe winning, the World Cup.
Switzerland's Blatter is perhaps a more likely European candidate, and, as FIFA's general-secretary, can claim to know the ins and outs of the organisation better than his potential rivals.
His current contract expires after the France finals, just when Havelange is due to go.
And finally there is Beckenbauer, who would undoubtably be the people's choice in Europe.

The Kaiser's credentials are undisputed. He is the only man to have won the World Cup as both player and coach and is respected across the world for his intelligent approach to the game. At 51, he is also young enough to pilot world football well into the next century.
Beckenbauer has already said he will quit as president of Bayern next year but has yet to announce what he plans to do next.

"I have watched all that has happened lately very closely and have spoken to certain people at the highest levels," he said when asked recently about the job as FIFA's overlord. "But then I am in touch with them regularly on football matters.
"When I leave Bayern I must be certain the next move is the right one. All I will say is I would not exclude taking over as president of FIFA."
